p: (1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and the Legislature of a State may make laws for the whole or any part of the State.
(2) No law made by Parliament shall be deemed to be invalid on the ground that it would have extra-territorial operation.
245.s: Parliament can make laws for all or part of India, and a State Legislature can make laws for all or part of its State. A law made by Parliament is not invalid just because it operates outside India's territory.

p: (1) Notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3), Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “Union List”).

(2) Notwithstanding anything in clause (3), Parliament, and, subject to clause (1), the Legislature of any State {1}*** also, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List III in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “Concurrent List”).

(3) Subject to clauses (1) and (2), the Legislature of any State {1}*** has exclusive power to make laws for such State or any part thereof with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List II in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the “State List”).

(4) Parliament has power to make laws with respect to any matter for any part of the territory of India not included {2}[in a State] notwithstanding that such matter is a matter enumerated in the State List.
f: The words and letters "specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
Subs. by s. 29 and Sch., ibid., for "in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule" (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
246.s: Only Parliament can make laws on Union List subjects and only a State Legislature on State List subjects for its State, while both can legislate on Concurrent List subjects, all set out in the Seventh Schedule. Parliament can also legislate on State List subjects for any part of India not in a State.
k: union list state list concurrent list
who can make laws on what subject
fh: specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule
in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule

p: (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in articles 246 and 254, Parliament, and, subject to clause (2), the Legislature of every State, have power to make laws with respect to goods and services tax imposed by the Union or by such State.
(2) Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to goods and services tax where the supply of goods, or of services, or both takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.

Explanation.—The provisions of this article, shall, in respect of goods and services tax referred to in clause (5) of article 279A, take effect from the date recommended by the Goods and Services Tax Council.]
f: Ins. by the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, s. 2 (w.e.f. 16-9-2016).
246A.s: Parliament and every State Legislature can make laws on goods and services tax imposed by the Union or that State. Only Parliament can make GST laws where goods or services are supplied in inter-State trade or commerce.

p: Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, Parliament may by law provide for the establishment of any additional courts for the better administration of laws made by Parliament or of any existing laws with respect to a matter enumerated in the Union List.
247.s: Parliament can, by law, set up additional courts to better administer laws made by Parliament or existing laws on Union List subjects.

p: (1) {1}[Subject to article 246A, Parliament] has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List.
(2) Such power shall include the power of making any law imposing a tax not mentioned in either of those Lists.
f: Subs. by the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, s. 3, for "Parliament" (w.e.f. 16-9-2016).
248.s: Only Parliament can make laws on any subject not listed in the Concurrent List or State List, including taxes not mentioned in either list, subject to the special rule on goods and services tax.

p: (1) Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, if the Council of States has declared by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest that Parliament should make laws with respect to {1}[goods and services tax provided under article 246A or] any matter enumerated in the State List specified in the resolution, it shall be lawful for Parliament to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India with respect to that matter while the resolution remains in force.
(2) A resolution passed under clause (1) shall remain in force for such period not exceeding one year as may be specified therein:

Provided that, if and so often as a resolution approving the continuance in force of any such resolution is passed in the manner provided in clause (1), such resolution shall continue in force for a further period of one year from the date on which under this clause it would otherwise have ceased to be in force.

(3) A law made by Parliament which Parliament would not but for the passing of a resolution under clause (1) have been competent to make shall, to the extent of the incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of a period of six months after the resolution has ceased to be in force, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration of the said period.
249.s: If the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution, backed by two-thirds of members present and voting, that it is in the national interest, Parliament can make laws on a State List subject or GST. The resolution lasts up to one year and can be renewed a year at a time, and such laws lapse six months after it ends.

p: (1) Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, Parliament shall, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, have power to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India with respect to {1}[goods and services tax provided under article 246A or] any of the matters enumerated in the State List.

(2) A law made by Parliament which Parliament would not but for the issue of a Proclamation of Emergency have been competent to make shall, to the extent of the incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of a period of six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration of the said period.
f: Ins. by the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, s. 5 (w.e.f. 16-9-2016).
250.s: While a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, Parliament can make laws for all or part of India on any State List subject or GST. Such laws stop having effect six months after the Emergency ends, except for things already done.

p: Nothing in articles 249 and 250 shall restrict the power of the Legislature of a State to make any law which under this Constitution it has power to make, but if any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament which Parliament has under either of the said articles power to make, the law made by Parliament, whether passed before or after the law made by the Legislature of the State, shall prevail, and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall to the extent of the repugnancy, but so long only as the law made by Parliament continues to have effect, be inoperative.
251.s: A State keeps its own law-making power despite Articles 249 and 250, but if a State law conflicts with a Parliament law made under them, the Parliament law prevails. The State law does not operate to that extent while the Parliament law is in effect.
k: conflict between central and state law

p: (1) If it appears to the Legislatures of two or more States to be desirable that any of the matters with respect to which Parliament has no power to make laws for the States except as provided in articles 249 and 250 should be regulated in such States by Parliament by law, and if resolutions to that effect are passed by all the Houses of the Legislatures of those States, it shall be lawful for Parliament to pass an act for regulating that matter accordingly, and any Act so passed shall apply to such States and to any other State by which it is adopted afterwards by resolution passed in that behalf by the House or, where there are two Houses, by each of the Houses of the Legislature of that State.

(2) Any Act so passed by Parliament may be amended or repealed by an Act of Parliament passed or adopted in like manner but shall not, as respects any State to which it applies, be amended or repealed by an Act of the Legislature of that State.
252.s: If the Legislatures of two or more States pass resolutions asking Parliament to make a law on a matter it normally cannot legislate on for States, Parliament can do so for them, and other States can adopt it by resolution. Only Parliament, acting the same way, can amend or repeal it, not the States.
k: states ask parliament to make law
law for two or more states

p: Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, Parliament has power to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international conference, association or other body.
253.s: Parliament can make laws for all or part of India to implement any treaty, agreement or convention with other countries, or any decision taken at an international conference, association or other body.

p: (1) If any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament which Parliament is competent to enact, or to any provision of an existing law with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List, then, subject to the provisions of clause (2), the law made by Parliament, whether passed before or after the law made by the Legislature of such State, or, as the case may be, the existing law, shall prevail and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void.

(2) Where a law made by the Legislature of a State {1}*** with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List contains any provision repugnant to the provisions of an earlier law made by Parliament or an existing law with respect to that matter, then, the law so made by the Legislature of such State shall, if it has been reserved for the consideration of the President and has received his assent, prevail in that State:

Provided that nothing in this clause shall prevent Parliament from enacting at any time any law with respect to the same matter including a law adding to, amending, varying or repealing the law so made by the Legislature of the State.
f: The words and letters "specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
254.s: If a State law conflicts with a Parliament law, or with an existing law on a Concurrent List subject, the Parliament or existing law prevails and the State law is void to that extent. A conflicting State law on a Concurrent subject prevails in that State with the President's assent, but Parliament can still change it.
fh: specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule

p: No Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of a State {1}***, and no provision in any such Act, shall be invalid by reason only that some recommendation or previous sanction required by this Constitution was not given, if assent to that Act was given—
(a) where the recommendation required was that of the Governor, either by the Governor or by the President;
(b) where the recommendation required was that of the Rajpramukh, either by the Rajpramukh or by the President;
(c) where the recommendation or previous sanction required was that of the President, by the President.
f: The words and letters "specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
255.s: An Act of Parliament or a State Legislature is not invalid only because a recommendation or prior sanction was missing, if assent came from the Governor or President (for a Governor's recommendation), the Rajpramukh or President (for a Rajpramukh's), or the President (for his own).
fh: specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule

p: The executive power of every State shall be so exercised as to ensure compliance with the laws made by Parliament and any existing laws which apply in that State, and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of such directions to a State as may appear to the Government of India to be necessary for that purpose:
256.s: Every State must use its executive power to ensure that laws made by Parliament and existing laws applying in that State are followed, and the Union can give a State any directions the Government of India finds necessary for this.

p: (1) The executive power of every State shall be so exercised as not to impede or prejudice the exercise of the executive power of the Union, and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of such directions to a State as may appear to the Government of India to be necessary for that purpose.

(2) The executive power of the Union shall also extend to the giving of directions to a State as to the construction and maintenance of means of communication declared in the direction to be of national or military importance:

Provided that nothing in this clause shall be taken as restricting the power of Parliament to declare highways or waterways to be national highways or national waterways or the power of the Union with respect to the highways or waterways so declared or the power of the Union to construct and maintain means of communication as part of its functions with respect to naval, military and air force works.
(3) The executive power of the Union shall also extend to the giving of directions to a State as to the measures to be taken for the protection of the railways within the State.

(4) Where in carrying out any direction given to a State under clause (2) as to the construction or maintenance of any means of communication or under clause (3) as to the measures to be taken for the protection of any railway, costs have been incurred in excess of those which would have been incurred in the discharge of the normal duties of the State if such direction had not been given, there shall be paid by the Government of India to the State such sum as may be agreed, or, in default of agreement, as may be determined by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India, in respect of the extra costs so incurred by the State.
257.s: States must use their executive power without obstructing the Union's, and the Government of India can direct them to ensure this. It can also direct States to build and maintain communications of national or military importance and to protect railways, paying extra costs as agreed or as fixed by an arbitrator the Chief Justice of India appoints.
k: roads of national or military importance

f: Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 43 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977).
257A.st: Omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 33 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).

p: (1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may, with the consent of the Government of a State, entrust either conditionally or unconditionally to that Government or to its officers functions in relation to any matter to which the executive power of the Union extends.

(2) A law made by Parliament which applies in any State may, notwithstanding that it relates to a matter with respect to which the Legislature of the State has no power to make laws, confer powers and impose duties, or authorise the conferring of powers and the imposition of duties, upon the State or officers and authorities thereof.

(3) Where by virtue of this article powers and duties have been conferred or imposed upon a State or officers or authorities thereof, there shall be paid by the Government of India to the State such sum as may be agreed, or, in default of agreement, as may be determined by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India, in respect of any extra costs of administration incurred by the State in connection with the exercise of those powers and duties.
258.s: With a State government's consent, the President can hand over Union functions to that government or its officers, with or without conditions. A law of Parliament can also give powers and duties to a State, and the Government of India pays the extra administrative costs, as agreed or as fixed by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India.

p: Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the Governor of a State may, with the consent of the Government of India, entrust either conditionally or unconditionally to that Government or to its officers functions in relation to any matter to which the executive power of the State extends.]
f: Ins. by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 18 (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
258A.s: With the consent of the Government of India, a State's Governor can hand over State functions to the Government of India or its officers, with or without conditions.
k: governor hand over powers to union

259.st: Omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).

p: The Government of India may by agreement with the Government of any territory not being part of the territory of India undertake any executive, legislative or judicial functions vested in the Government of such territory, but every such agreement shall be subject to, and governed by, any law relating to the exercise of foreign jurisdiction for the time being in force.
260.s: The Government of India can, by agreement with the government of a territory outside India, take on that territory's executive, legislative or judicial functions. Such agreements must follow the law on foreign jurisdiction in force at the time.

p: (1) Full faith and credit shall be given throughout the territory of India to public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and of every State.

(2) The manner in which and the conditions under which the acts, records and proceedings referred to in clause (1) shall be proved and the effect thereof determined shall be as provided by law made by Parliament.
(3) Final judgments or orders delivered or passed by civil courts in any part of the territory of India shall be capable of execution anywhere within that territory according to law.
261.s: Public acts, records and court proceedings of the Union and every State get full faith and credit across India, with their proof and effect set by Parliament by law. Final civil court judgments or orders can be enforced anywhere in India according to law.
k: enforce civil court judgment in another state

p: (1) Parliament may by law provide for the adjudication of any dispute or complaint with respect to the use, distribution or control of the waters of, or in, any inter-State river or river valley.

(2) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may by law provide that neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall exercise jurisdiction in respect of any such dispute or complaint as is referred to in clause (1).
262.s: Parliament can make laws to settle disputes or complaints about the use, distribution or control of the waters of inter-State rivers or river valleys. It can also bar the Supreme Court and all other courts from hearing such disputes.

p: If at any time it appears to the President that the public interests would be served by the establishment of a Council charged with the duty of—
(a) inquiring into and advising upon disputes which may have arisen between States;
(b) investigating and discussing subjects in which some or all of the States, or the Union and one or more of the States, have a common interest; or
(c) making recommendations upon any such subject and, in particular, recommendations for the better co-ordination of policy and action with respect to that subject,
it shall be lawful for the President by order to establish such a Council, and to define the nature of the duties to be performed by it and its organisation and procedure.
263.s: If the President thinks it serves the public interest, the President can by order set up a Council to advise on disputes between States, study subjects of common interest, and recommend better policy coordination. The order sets its duties, organisation and procedure.

why: Minerva Mills (1980) held that setting aside Articles 14 and 19 for a whole class of laws destroys the basic structure; Coelho (2007) treats the core of Articles 14, 19 and 21 as the test for Ninth Schedule laws.
Coelho (2007) called Article 32 "an important and integral part of the basic structure", and L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that judicial review under it cannot be ousted.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that the High Courts' power of judicial review under Article 226, and their superintendence under Article 227, are part of the inviolable basic structure.
Minerva Mills (1980) held that a limited amending power is itself a basic feature, so Parliament cannot amend this article to make its power unlimited.

The NJAC case (2015) struck down the Ninety-ninth Amendment's new method of appointing judges as a breach of judicial independence, so the core of how judges are appointed is part of the basic structure.
Names India as a Union of States. Abolishing the Union or the States would undo federalism and India's sovereignty, both part of the framework.
This is the hook for testing laws against fundamental rights. Courts have said the power to test legislation "can never be ousted".
Core guarantees against discrimination and untouchability. Coelho (2007) named Article 15 among the rights forming part of the basic structure.
Freedom of religion is the main textual home of secularism, which the Court has repeatedly called a basic feature.
Judicial review by the High Courts, held to be basic, depends on the High Courts existing.
Adult suffrage is the foundation of democracy and free and fair elections.

Kesavananda Bharati (Khanna J) held that, apart from the part that relates to the basic structure, the Preamble does not limit the power to amend. Balram Singh (2024) rejected a challenge to adding "socialist" and "secular" in 1976.
Defines "the State" against which fundamental rights are enforced; gutting it would hollow out the rights.
Equality of opportunity in public employment is part of the equality code, though clauses on reservation have been changed and upheld.
Basic protections of personal liberty and fair criminal process, closely tied to Article 21.
Bans on forced labour and child labour in hazardous work relate to human dignity; no case has tested their repeal.
Religious freedom of groups and the bar on State religious instruction carry secularism into practice.
Minority rights to culture and to run educational institutions support pluralism and secularism.
The Directive to separate the judiciary from the executive expresses separation of powers and judicial independence.
An elected President as head of state is part of the republican form of government.
How the President is elected. Entrenched: changing it needs ratification by half the States.
Extent of Union executive power, one half of the federal balance. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
Ministers advise the President and answer collectively to the Lok Sabha: the core of parliamentary government.
An elected Parliament, with the States represented in it. Representation of the States is entrenched.
Fixed terms for the Houses guarantee periodic elections.
Parliament cannot discuss a judge's conduct except on a motion for removal, a rule tied to judicial independence.
Judges' salaries cannot be cut to their disadvantage while in office, a guard on judicial independence.
Courts of record with power to punish contempt, part of the courts' ability to make their orders effective.
The Supreme Court settles disputes between the Union and the States, a federal safeguard.
Special leave to appeal lets the Supreme Court correct any court or tribunal, central to access to justice.
Each State has its own executive, part of the federal structure.
Extent of State executive power. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
State ministers advise the Governor and answer to the Assembly: parliamentary government at State level.
An elected State Legislature with fixed terms, needed for both democracy and federalism.
Transfers of High Court judges. The NJAC case struck down the 2014 change to this article as part of the same scheme.
High Court control over the subordinate courts keeps the district judiciary independent of the executive.
The division of law-making power between Parliament and the States. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
No tax without the authority of law, a basic rule-of-law guarantee.
An independent Election Commission conducts elections; without it free and fair elections would be at risk.
A single electoral roll with no exclusion on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex.
The right to education. Its insertion was upheld, but no case says whether removing it would breach the basic structure.
The welfare-state directives most closely tied to the balance between Parts III and IV. Removing them might upset that balance; untested.
Courts cannot question the validity of legislative proceedings on grounds of procedure. Touches both separation of powers and judicial review.
Binding precedent and the power to do complete justice. Important to the Court's role, but not tested as basic.
An independent auditor of public accounts supports the rule of law and accountability; untested.
Organisational rules for the High Courts. Some core is needed for judicial review, but the details can change.
President's Rule. Its use is reviewable (Bommai), and abuse can damage federalism and democracy, but the article itself is not part of the basic structure.
Suspension of rights during emergency. Since 1978, Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended; widening this power again could touch the core of rights.
Parliament already changes State boundaries by ordinary law; the federal structure survives individual changes.
Citizenship rules. Parliament already controls citizenship by law under Article 11.
These shield certain laws from fundamental rights challenges. Removing them would restore rights, not damage the structure.
Powers to adapt or restrict rights for armed forces and martial law; administrative in nature.
Individual Directive Principles. The balance between Parts III and IV is basic, but no single directive has been held essential.
Fundamental duties were added in 1976 and are not enforceable in court.
Detailed rules on the President, Vice-President and conduct of business. Can change without touching a basic feature.
Detailed rules on Parliament's membership, officers and procedure.
Legislative and financial procedure, and ordinances. Can be redesigned without damaging democracy itself.
Organisation and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court beyond its core review power. Many have been amended before.
Form and reporting of public accounts.
Detailed rules on Governors and State executive business.
Detailed rules on State Legislatures, their officers and members.
State legislative and financial procedure, assent to Bills and ordinances.
Detailed rules on High Court judges and jurisdiction beyond the core review power.
Appointment and rules for district judges and subordinate courts.
How Union territories are governed. Parliament has changed this often.
Panchayats, added in 1992. Local democracy, but not part of the original framework or any holding.
Administration of Scheduled and Tribal Areas.
Specific rules within the division of legislative power. Entrenched where in Chapter I of Part XI, but individually changeable.
Administrative relations between the Union and the States.
Distribution of revenues and the Finance Commission. Revised many times, including by GST in 2016.
Freedom of trade within India and its exceptions.
Civil services and Public Service Commissions.
Tribunals may exist; what is part of the basic structure is the High Courts' and Supreme Court's review over them, not these articles.
Election law-making and the bar on courts during elections.
Reservations in legislatures and services, commissions and lists. Many have sunset clauses or have been amended; upheld when changed.
Linguistic minority protections and the Hindi directive.
Emergency powers. The articles themselves are not part of the basic structure.
Transitional provisions continuing earlier laws, courts and officers.
The right to property. Kesavananda Bharati (Khanna J) held it is not part of the basic structure.
Temporary and special provisions for particular States. Several have been changed or ended, and the changes upheld.
Abolition of titles. An equality measure, but minor; no case suggests it is essential.
Equal justice and free legal aid, the directive most closely tied to effective access to justice.
Concurrent power over GST, added in 2016. A specific fiscal arrangement within federalism.
Interpretation clause for the Part on finance.
Co-operative societies, added in 2011. Detailed regulatory rules.
Salaries of members and rules of procedure and language in Parliament.
Definitions, interpretation, short title, commencement, the Hindi text and repeals.
Lists the States and Union territories. Parliament changes it by ordinary law under Articles 3 and 4.
Salaries and allowances of constitutional office-holders.
Forms of oaths, including the oath to uphold the Constitution.
Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats. Entrenched, but the numbers change by amendment.
Autonomous districts in the North-East; amended many times.
The Union, State and Concurrent Lists as a scheme are the core of federalism. Individual entries are changed often.
Laws shielded from fundamental rights challenges. Removing the shield would not damage the structure.
The anti-defection law, upheld in Kihoto Hollohan. Repealing it would not breach a basic feature.

democracy.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); S.R. Bommai (1994)
democracy.s: Government by elected representatives, with an elected head of state.

secular.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); S.R. Bommai (1994); I.R. Coelho (2007); Balram Singh (2024)
secular.s: The State treats all religions equally and has no religion of its own.

federal.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); S.R. Bommai (1994)
federal.s: Power is divided between the Union and the States, and the States are not mere agents of the Centre.

sop.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); I.R. Coelho (2007)
sop.s: Legislature, executive and judiciary each keep their own sphere.

rol.c: P. Sambamurthy (1986); I.R. Coelho (2007); Raj Narain (1975)
rol.s: Government acts under law, and its decisions can be tested by independent courts.

equality.t: Equality and the core of fundamental rights
equality.s: The core of Articles 14, 19 and 21, and of each fundamental right, cannot be taken away.

balance.t: Balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
balance.s: Parts III and IV must be kept in harmony; neither may be made to swallow the other.

jr.s: The High Courts and the Supreme Court must be able to test laws and government action against the Constitution.

indep.s: Judges must be appointed, and do their work, free of control by the executive.

access.s: People must be able to reach a court to enforce their rights. The right to go to the Supreme Court under Article 32 is itself part of the basic structure.

amend.s: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, but cannot use that power to destroy its identity or make the power unlimited.

sovereign.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973; Shelat and Grover JJ, Hegde and Mukherjea JJ)
sovereign.s: India is a sovereign Union; its unity and integrity are part of the framework.

at.KB: pp. 280-281 (Shelat and Grover JJ) and p. 322 (Hegde and Mukherjea JJ)

parl.s: Ministers are drawn from and answerable to an elected legislature.

elections.c: Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975, Khanna J)
elections.s: Elections must be free and fair, and their results open to lawful challenge.

supremacy.s: Every organ of the State is bound by the Constitution.
